board-overview.title: Flux V1: buses and chips
board-overview.alt: Block diagram of the Flux V1 board: the ESP32-S3 connects over one SPI bus to the MAX22200 solenoid driver and the TLE92466ED proportional driver, over a second SPI bus to the ADS7952 ADC, over its internal ADC to the NTC thermistor and bus-voltage divider, over TWAI to the CAN transceiver, over UART to the FDO2 probe and to a WS2812 LED.
board-overview.description: The ESP32-S3 on the left runs all the software. Each arrow to the right is one bus or signal, labelled with the GPIOs it uses. One SPI bus is shared by the two valve drivers: the MAX22200 (eight solenoid channels) and the TLE92466ED (six proportional, current-controlled channels), each with its own chip select and its own control and fault lines. A second SPI bus is dedicated to the ADS7952 12-channel external ADC. The ESP32-S3's own ADC reads the NTC thermistor and the bus-voltage divider. TWAI goes to the CAN transceiver, a UART is reserved for the FDO2 oxygen probe, and one data line drives the WS2812 status LED. The layout is drawn by hand; every GPIO number, ADC channel, chip select and SPI mode is read from the functional pin map and the comms manager, so a pin change rebuilds this figure.

hal-layers.title: Flux V1 HAL, layer by layer
hal-layers.alt: Layer stack of the Flux V1 HAL: application, the Flux facade, 7 managers, 5 hf-core handlers, 6 chip drivers, and the interface wrap on ESP-IDF and the ESP32-S3.
hal-layers.description: From top to bottom, each layer only calls the one under it. Your application asks the facade singleton for the managers. The managers (one per board function) own the hf-core handlers, which wrap one chip driver each; a manager may also use a driver directly. Drivers talk to hardware only through the interface classes of the internal interface wrap, whose ESP32 implementations sit on ESP-IDF. Every name in a band is read from the code: the managers from the facade's member references, the handlers, drivers and interface classes from the managers' and handlers' #include lines.

init-order.title: Flux::EnsureInitialized()
init-order.alt: Initialisation order: NvsManager, CommChannelsManager, GpioManager are required; then ValveManager, AdcManager, LedManager, TemperatureManager are best effort and only produce warnings if they fail.
init-order.description: Left to right, then the second row. The facade initialises the managers one at a time, in the order of the calls in its init function. The first group is required: if any of them fails, EnsureInitialized() returns false and the application should not continue. The second group is best effort: a failure there is logged as a warning, the manager stays unavailable and the system reports itself as degraded, so a bench with only some chips fitted still comes up. The order and the required / best-effort split are read from the init function, which returns false only in the required branches.

manager-dependencies.title: Managers, handlers and drivers
manager-dependencies.alt: Graph from each manager to the hf-core handlers it uses and from each handler to the chip driver it wraps: ValveManager to the MAX22200 and TLE92466ED handlers, AdcManager to the ADS7952 handler, TemperatureManager to the NTC and MCP9700 handlers, and LedManager directly to the WS2812 driver.
manager-dependencies.description: Managers on the left, hf-core handlers in the middle, chip drivers on the right. An arrow means "includes and uses": a manager owns the handler it points at, and each handler wraps exactly one driver. ValveManager owns both valve drivers (MAX22200 for the solenoid channels, TLE92466ED for the proportional channels), AdcManager owns the ADS7952 external ADC, and TemperatureManager owns the NTC and MCP9700 sensor handlers. LedManager uses its driver directly, without a handler. Managers with no arrow (communication buses, GPIO, NVS) talk to the interface wrap only.
